cs.LG / 89 / 2611.30868
MUNDO: a multiresolution generative framework for temporal downscaling
Aymeric Delefosse, Manon Tavernier, Julie Keisler, Anastase Charantonis, Dominique Béréziat
cs.LG · physics.ao-ph
Abstract
Dynamical systems are often observed at coarse temporal resolution through sparse states or temporal aggregates, leaving the underlying fine-scale trajectories unresolved. Recovering these trajectories requires probabilistic models that capture the unresolved variability while remaining consistent with the observations. We present MUNDO (Multiresolution UNified DOwnscaling), a generative framework for temporal downscaling under general linear observation operators. MUNDO introduces a null-space parameterization that enforces exact observation consistency in a single network evaluation, unifying temporal interpolation and disaggregation. To capture complex multiscale dynamics, we leverage reverse Markov learning to factorize the observation operator into a hierarchy of successive coarsenings. Each level models only the degrees of freedom lost between adjacent resolutions. We evaluate MUNDO on two-scale Lorenz-96, four two-dimensional physical systems, and multivariate ERA5 reanalysis over Europe, for both temporal interpolation and disaggregation. Across datasets and tasks, MUNDO generally outperforms flow-based baselines. Single-step MUNDO achieves strong predictive skill, while recursive MUNDO generally improves temporal realism and ensemble calibration, with better spread-skill agreement and predictive coverage.

cs.LG / 90 / 2611.30881
AnchorCredit: Output-Anchored Credit Assignment for Structured Generation with Multiple Verifiable Rewards
Gen Li, Pengyang Xie, Xiao Xiao, Chuanzhi Tong, Ziyang Ji, Zhigang Xu, Huiwen Bai, Zihao Xing, Yanxiang Zhou, Yifei Yuan, Xiaoqing Wang
cs.LG
Abstract
In Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and related methods typically compute group-relative advantages from response rewards and broadcast the same advantage to every generated token in a response to guide policy updates. However, we identify a systematic problem of cross-component credit misassignment in tasks with multiple verifiable results, such as joint multi-attribute prediction: low rewards for some components can penalize a well-performing component and its associated reasoning. To address this problem, we propose AnchorCredit. The method uses the policy model's attention from output anchors to preceding reasoning sentences to estimate sentence-component associations and assign component-specific advantages to the relevant reasoning, without additional relevance annotations or a separate relevance discriminator. To support the study of credit assignment with multiple verifiable rewards, we construct ProductAttr, a benchmark of 7,200 real product image-text samples. Experiments show that AnchorCredit outperforms existing baselines on this benchmark. Experiments on the public Nutrition5k dataset further support the method's effectiveness in this setting.

Predicting Rare-Mode Collapse in Recursive Generative Training from Single-Generation Calibration
Jingyao Zhang, Mingyu Du, Lu Han
cs.LG · cs.AI
Abstract
Recursive generative training can preserve sample counts in a rare region while silently eroding its characteristic core. Mapping this finite-horizon collapse across real-data quotas, rare prevalences, and feedback perturbations via exhaustive multi-generation chains is computationally prohibitive. We develop a decoupled framework that forecasts multi-generation collapse probabilities and locates operating risk boundaries from independent single-generation conditional fits alone. Pairing an exact three-source multinomial count law with single-generation response banks propagates count marginals in closed form, backed by explicit calibration-error and boundary-resolution bounds. For additive Gaussian perturbations, we further prove that equal-variance all-row and sparse policies reverse their boundary-crossing order at a unique hyperplane distance. Across a 2,178-setting count benchmark, exact propagation cuts risk mean absolute error (MAE) from 1.85 to 0.49 percentage points (pp). Across ten two-dimensional learners, calibration achieves 2.60--5.69~pp six-round core MAE on nine stationary learners (65--81\% below an unperturbed baseline), diagnoses non-stationary outlier drift in standard DDIM (16.38~pp) via a stability probe, and resolves the predicted six-round geometric reversal. On Fashion-MNIST latent flow-matching chains, calibration outperforms direct-chain Gaussian-process interpolation at lower fit budgets and tracks the 20\% latent-perturbation boundary shift (3.14 versus 10.78~pp MAE for proportion copying) driven by opposing inflow to the rare region and outflow from its core.

cs.LG / 92 / 2611.30916
TrialAgentBench: Evaluating AI Agents for Clinical-Trial Analysis and Long-Horizon Drug-Development Decisions
Bradley Segal, William Bolton, Philip Torr, David Clifton, Lei Clifton
cs.LG · cs.AI
Abstract
Clinical drug development is a long-horizon, high-stakes process requiring sequential decisions based on information that costs money and time to acquire. AI agents have demonstrated capabilities for scientific analysis, but there is no established way to evaluate them on these decisions, as real trials are expensive, involve people, and never reveal the counterfactual. We introduce TrialAgentBench, a benchmark for evaluating AI agents on clinical trial analysis and drug development decision-making using simulated trials where the truth is known, embedded within the data records of a fictional drug sponsor. We publicly release nearly 3,500 tasks, varying from analysing a single trial to managing multi-phase programmes with budget and time constraints. We score each analysis by rerunning its code on new trials, and each programme by the value its decisions achieve. Across 24 closed- and open-weight models, the strongest agents can analyse raw, messy trial records to within 6% of a process-aware analysis, even when an assumption is violated, with 95% confidence intervals containing the true effect 94--95% of the time. Over the prior year, the best model improved from 19% above this analysis, with serious misses on 15% of tasks, to 3.5% and 1%. What limits them is decision-making from evidence under uncertainty: when to correct, what evidence to buy, when to stop. The strongest agents are overly careful, correcting on 83% of tasks with equal recording errors, where it is unnecessary. On drug programmes, the best agent has substantial headroom, reaching 48% of the value an oracle achieves against 58% for a rule-based developer, with others falling 24 to 66% short. Model generations show ongoing improvements in handling data and evidence, with substantial variation. The strongest models can act as competent analysts, but do not yet make reliable long-horizon decisions.

cs.LG / 93 / 2611.30939
Beyond Patching: Consistent Circuit Discovery via Gradient Spectral Analysis
Yujie Zhang, Tianyi Zhao, Guanghui Min, Chen Chen
cs.LG · cs.AI
Abstract
Mechanistic interpretability seeks to reverse-engineer neural networks by identifying small, faithful subgraphs--circuits--that implement specific behaviors. The dominant paradigm scores each unit by replacing its clean activation with a corrupted counterpart as causal intervention. While effective, this approach rests on a brittle prerequisite: the structure prompt pairs are task-specific, expensive to engineer, and silently couple the discovered circuit to prompt-design choices. In this work, we propose Spectral Circuit Analysis (SCA), a gradient-spectral pipeline that achieves consistent circuit discovery along both axes: stable across input formulations of the same task, and natively exposing structure shared across tasks. Our contributions are threefold. First, we provide a counterfactual-free reframing of circuit discovery: causally relevant directions are recoverable from the spectral structure of forward gradients across paraphrases, with leading directions concentrating task signal and trailing ones absorbing paraphrase noise, yielding circuits tied to the task rather than the prompt. Second, we introduce SCA, a block-wise SVD pipeline that extracts a task subspace per architectural block and redistributes spectral energy onto constituent units via a consistency-weighted share, producing per-unit rankings competitive with attribution-patching baselines under strictly less supervision. Finally, on twelve circuit-discovery tasks in GPT-2 Small and Pythia-160M, SCA performs comparably or exceeds EAP-family methods under the standard recovery-score protocol and recovers IOI canonical heads with Precision@K = 1.0 in top-10 slices on GPT-2 Small; the same machinery extends to a unified cross-task analysis classifying units as universal, family-shared, or task-specific and exposing compositional structure invisible to per-task analyses.

cs.LG / 94 / 2611.30970
Explanation Selection in Abductive Learning
En-Hao Gao, Yuan Jiang
cs.LG
Abstract
Abductive learning (ABL) offers a promising framework that connects machine learning and logical reasoning in a mutually beneficial loop. However, this bidirectional feedback can also reinforce incorrect concept semantics, since different interpretations of intermediate concepts may explain the same observed reasoning outcomes. Static analyses characterize this ambiguity but leave open which explanation training selects and whether its labels can still be corrected. We develop a dynamical analysis of a fixed-feature binary ABL model that links the local stability of competing explanations to differences in their concept labels. We prove that Gram matrices with identical spectra can select different explanations even under the same supervision, objective, and initialization. When any two compatible explanations differ in at least two labels, legal evidence above one half guarantees during training that admissible changes in optimization geometry preserve the selected explanation. Even when only the true explanation satisfies all constraints under a shared predictor, training can still converge to a finite attracting state whose hard predictions violate some constraints and mislabel concepts. Experiments on visual ABL tasks verify these predictions, including wrong attraction from random initializations under identifiable supervision, and show that in ordinary end-to-end training SGD and Adam select different explanations of the same supervision, while unseen concept accuracy drops relative to true-concept references as training concept errors grow.

cs.LG / 95 / 2611.31015
Can Latent Reasoning Drive LLM Outputs Without a Trace?
Tomer Ashuach, Zorik Gekhman, Avi Caciularu, Ori Ram, Jonathan Herzig
cs.LG · cs.AI · cs.CL
Abstract
LLMs typically solve complex tasks with chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, which is also the main tool for monitoring them for misaligned behavior. However, standard transformers can also solve tasks with complete latent reasoning (CLR), carrying out the whole task internally and outputting only the final answer. Theory bounds the depth of CLR, the number of sequential steps it can carry out, and recent work measured it to be shallow. In this work, we ask whether CLR is deep enough for a model to pursue a hidden objective that requires reasoning. Such a model would generate a CoT that appears to solve the given task, while a latent multi-step computation decides its answer based on the hidden objective. First, we show that a simple auxiliary loss allows models to solve a multi-step task latently at least 5x deeper than previously reported. Then, in two common tasks, decision-making and code generation, we train a model to pursue such a hidden objective, which decides a loan or plants a vulnerability. The model's CoT justifies the output with no trace of the hidden objective, and a strong LLM monitor does not flag it. Finally, using activation patching, we find that the latent computation is completed before the model generates its CoT, which takes no part in it. Altogether, we show that a hidden objective that requires reasoning can go unseen by a monitor that reads only the output.

cs.LG / 96 / 2611.31032
Black-Box Comparator-Adaptive Network Regret
Tomas Ortega, Hamid Jafarkhani
cs.LG · eess.SP · math.OC
Abstract
We study comparator-adaptive decentralized online learning with network regret, which evaluates each node's prediction on the loss of every node in the network. We show that existing gossip-based algorithms are fundamentally limited for this task, and cannot achieve sublinear network regret with only one gossip step per decision round. To prove this, we construct a two-node counterexample, which shows that gossip-based algorithms can produce exponential regret despite bounded disagreement, resolving a previously open question in the literature. We then introduce a black-box reduction, which uses local learners with sublinear comparator-adaptive regret to obtain sublinear comparator-adaptive network regret. Each node exchanges predictions with its neighbors once per decision round, and a universal choice of edge weights works on every connected undirected graph without graph preprocessing. We also characterize admissible edge weights and show how weights adapted to the graph improve the regret bound. For example, for the complete graph, this improvement is quadratic in the number of nodes. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data illustrate the counterexamples we propose and compare the reduction with decentralized baselines.

RoFE: Rotated Frozen Embeddings for Low-Data Multimodal Tabular Learning
Yihao Qiao, Jiajian Ma, Wushuang Rui, Abhishek Jha, Aarti Darji, Yiqiu Shen
cs.LG · cs.CV · stat.ML
Abstract
Multimodal tabular learning combines tabular data with images and text, often in settings where labeled data are scarce. Tabular foundation models such as prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) offer a promising solution via in-context learning without task-specific training. However, modern image and text encoders produce embeddings with hundreds or thousands of dimensions, far exceeding the number of features encountered during PFN pretraining. Existing approaches bridge this gap using principal component analysis (PCA) to compress frozen embeddings. Surprisingly, we find that this PCA interface can underperform simple linear classifiers when labeled examples are scarce, even though PFNs are designed for small datasets. We identify the underlying failure mechanism: the PFN's per-column standardization removes the variances of the PCA scores. When the PCA keeps every direction of the labeled examples, the examples collapse into a regular simplex in which all pairwise distances are equal. To address this problem, we propose Rotated Frozen Embeddings (RoFE), a training-free method that rotates PCA scores before PFN inference. We theoretically show that rotation makes the column variances nearly equal, so that standardization approximately preserves the embedding geometry. Across image and text classification tasks, encoders, and tabular foundation models, RoFE improves low-data performance over the PCA interface and outperforms baselines that require task-specific training. The improvements also extend to regression.

Attention Temperature Confounds Zero-Shot Context Extension
Ruben Navasardyan
cs.LG · cs.AI · cs.CL
Abstract
A training-time attention change is usually judged for zero-shot context extension against a dense baseline beyond the training length at the default temperature, $τ= 1$. The outcome depends on how miscalibrated the baseline is there: the share of perplexity it recovers when its logits are sharpened by one scalar. Under the standard recipe (fp32 master weights), an 8k-trained baseline is 8-15% miscalibrated at 30k in three seed-paired 365M twins; in one of them this makes the block-sparse-trained twin look 7% better, which calibration removes. In pure-bf16 training without master weights the miscalibration is several times larger: an AdamW step ($β_2 = 0.95$) on a gain initialised at 1.0 is below half the bf16 spacing at peak learning rates under $1.7\times10^{-3}$, so gains never move (22 checkpoints), the baseline is 37-58% miscalibrated, and block-sparse pretraining, attention dropout and ALiBi look 6-35% better. Calibrating one temperature per model and length removes all three advantages, leaves ALiBi 5% behind RoPE and keeps part of the gain of a positive control, NTK-aware scaling. Unfreezing the gains reverses the block-sparse advantage at 365M and removes 71-89% of it at 1.2B. We recommend reporting extension results at calibrated temperatures and checking that normalisation gains moved.

cs.LG / 99 / 2611.31154
Attention Latent Feedback
Xuyuan Xiong, Siyu Chen, Mengzhao Chen, Yue Su, Zhuoran Yang, Ping Luo, Xihui Liu
cs.LG
Abstract
During autoregressive decoding, the deeper representations of the previous token have already been computed, yet shallow layers at the current token cannot read them directly because standard self-attention connects positions only at the same depth. We introduce Attention Latent Feedback (ALF), an architecture that allows every sublayer to attend to the outputs of the deeper layers at the previous position. Training unrolls this cross-position recurrence into two parallel passes, whereas decoding remains single-pass using cached previous-token states. Across mixture-of-experts models with up to 4.0B parameters, ALF lowers held-out loss by 0.022-0.024 nats over the standard residual with about 1.1% decoding FLOP overhead, and consistently outperforms prior final-state feedback across all three scales on both standard and attention residual backbones. On MoE-1.6B, ALF matches a $1.38\times$ larger baseline token budget, and on MoE-4.0B it lifts average accuracy across seventeen downstream benchmarks from 45.1% to 47.0%. Analysis further reveals that intermediate and nearby deeper layers drive most of this benefit, allowing a fixed nearest-window variant to retain 89%-94% of the gain at linear read cost while learned attention widens its margin with scale.

EEG Decoding in Context: A Framework for Tuning-Free EEG Foundation Models
Hao-Run Cai, Si-Yang Liu, Han-Jia Ye, Hairong Zheng
cs.LG
Abstract
Electroencephalography (EEG) decoding is a central route toward brain-computer interfaces for communication, rehabilitation, cognitive assessment, and neurological monitoring. Recent EEG foundation models have substantially advanced reusable signal representations, but their downstream use still typically requires a task-specific decoder, gradient-based adaptation, and validation-driven model selection. We investigate a complementary foundation-model paradigm based on in-context learning: labeled EEG recordings define the decoding task as context, and new recordings are predicted without updating model parameters. We first pair raw EEG features with a pretrained general-purpose in-context predictor. This direct formulation provides a promising starting point, but its performance remains limited and unstable and does not generalize reliably across EEG paradigms. We find that suitable context construction can address these limitations by improving the effective signal-to-noise ratio and exposing temporal and spatial structure. Building on this insight, we introduce a general framework that combines EEG-specific context construction with a frozen in-context predictor and a metric-based context adaptation mechanism, which matches each downstream task to an appropriate context representation without relying on validation data. Across ten datasets spanning seven EEG decoding paradigms, our method achieves the highest mean BAcc among eleven specialized and fine-tuned EEG baselines, without task-specific parameter updates or validation-based model selection. This framework provides a practical path toward tuning-free EEG foundation models in which adaptation is expressed through context rather than parameter updates.

Learning Neurovascular Codes for EEG-to-fMRI Synthesis
Yiming Sun, Yifan Wang, Aosong Feng, Yijia Ma, Ben Cheng, Xurui Wang, Yufan He, Yucheng Tang, Qing Lyu, Daguang Xu, Pei-Fen Kuan, Mingzhou Ding, Wen Li, Chenyu You
cs.LG · cs.AI
Abstract
In this paper, we introduce Neurovascular Codes as shared EEG representations for fMRI generation. We first train a separate EEG encoder to predict each fMRI signal, learning target-specific temporal and spectral features from the same EEG window. After training, we freeze the encoders and project their concatenated hidden features into a shared neurovascular code. Conditioned on this code, stochastic interpolant transforms Gaussian noise into a vector of fMRI signals, allowing different responses to be sampled for the same EEG window. We evaluate our approach on eight public simultaneous EEG-fMRI datasets, including four resting-state and four task-based datasets with 61,646 volume-level pairs. Under within-subject and held-out-subject evaluation, our model improves average Pearson correlation over the strongest encoder baselines by 19.1% and 19.8%, respectively. The corresponding improvements over the strongest generator baselines are 18.8% and 47.9%. Beyond reconstruction accuracy, we also evaluate the generated signals using subject-identification classifiers trained on real fMRI. Our method achieves the highest mean accuracy among the evaluated generators. We hope that our work opens up new opportunities for cross-modal brain modeling.

cs.LG / 102 / 2611.31208
Matching Under Metric Privacy
Hongyi B. Hu, Dung Nguyen, M. Amin Rahimian
cs.LG · cs.CR · cs.SI · math.PR
Abstract
We study how to represent and randomize points in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space to obtain accurate bipartite matchings under metric privacy. Given $n$ private and $n$ public points, we analyze local mechanisms that randomize each private point or its distances to the public points. Using the public points' affine span, we construct a smaller representation that preserves all matching costs. When a trusted server receives the private points, we establish privacy and utility guarantees for Gumbel matching, which randomizes edge costs and releases only the assignment. Through upper bounds and worst-case constructions, we establish the tight rate $Θ\!\left(n\min\{d,\log n\}/\varepsilon\right)$ for expected cost above the nonprivate optimum. Benchmark experiments support $d\approx\log n$ as a practical guide to the transition between directly randomizing point coordinates and using Gumbel matching. Extensions to squared Euclidean costs enable private nonparametric two-sample hypothesis testing. These results show how the application's trust model guides representation and dimension choices for better utility: under local privacy, low-dimensional point representations reduce excess cost, while under central privacy, distance representations achieve the optimal rate even in high dimension.

cs.LG / 103 / 2611.31223
Agentic AI for Intent Management and Control in Autonomous Communication Networks
Burak Demirel, Yu Wang, Pablo Soldati
cs.LG
Abstract
Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven automation will help future mobile networks translate high-level network intents into concrete network optimization or control actions. However, existing approaches often focus on intent management and orchestration, leaving the adaptation of underlying network optimization and control functions largely unaddressed. This article proposes a triadic agentic AI framework that co-designs intent management and intent fulfillment through three agents: an interpreter, powered by a language model, that translates and refines intents into machine-readable optimization templates; an optimizer that adapts controller policies to intent specifications; and a controller that performs fast decision-making. We discuss the design space of each agent and how the workflow can be embedded across network architectural domains. Finally, we develop a concrete realization combining a language-model interpreter with Bayesian optimization for the optimizer and multi-objective reinforcement learning for the controller, and evaluate it in a radio resource management case study for differentiated connectivity. Results demonstrate how the agentic AI framework can connect high-level intents with runtime network control, showing adaptability of intent specifications and control policies to service requirements and changing network conditions.

How Far Can Linear Go? BiPert, a Unified Framework for Single-Cell Perturbation Modelling
Abhishek Sharma, Aleksej Zelezniak
cs.LG · q-bio.CB · q-bio.GN · q-bio.QM
Abstract
Understanding how genetic perturbations affect cellular behaviour is essential for studying gene function and regulatory mechanisms. Large-scale CRISPR screens measure these effects across thousands of genes, but cover relatively few cellular contexts. Predicting perturbation responses in unseen cell types and identifying perturbed genes from their transcriptional effects therefore remain challenging. Here, we show that both tasks can be addressed through a common linear decomposition of transcriptional responses into shared and perturbation-specific components. Building on this principle, we introduce BiPert, a simple linear framework for both forward perturbation prediction and inverse identification. For forward prediction, BiPert outperforms existing methods that use no external biological knowledge when predicting gene expression changes in unseen cell lines. Its few-shot extension, BiPert-FS, adapts to new cell lines using as few as ten measured perturbations. For inverse identification, BiPert-ID identifies perturbed genes from single-cell expression profiles, outperforming deep-learning methods in unseen cell lines and donors. We further show that perturbations whose effects transfer more consistently across cellular contexts are also easier to identify, even after controlling for perturbation effect size. Together, these results establish a connection between perturbation transfer and identification, and demonstrate that simple linear models provide strong, interpretable baselines for both tasks.

ABI: Actor-Free Behavior-Induced Representations for Zero-Shot Test-Time Guidance
Yifei Yao, Yude Zou, Guanbo Jiao, Jianming Ma, Xing Gao, Chunhua Shen
cs.RO · cs.LG
Abstract
Behavior-cloning policies show strong ability in sequential control by generating coherent multi-step action chunks, yet their purely imitative objective limits zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks. While offline reinforcement learning offers principled policy improvement, existing methods either require task-specific reward supervision or remain tied to a specific actor during critic training or policy deployment, inflating training cost and restricting cross-policy generalization. We observe that evaluating actions under the data-collecting behavior largely preserves their relative value ordering across target policies, offering a way around actor coupling. Combining this property with reward-free successor prediction, we propose Actor-Free Behavior-Induced Representations (ABI) to learn multi-horizon action-chunk representations from unlabeled trajectories without reward supervision or actor training. At test time, pairing the frozen representation with lightweight task readouts forms a chunk critic that guides target policies without parameter updates and transfers directly across distinct unseen policies. Our analysis establishes when the value ordering is preserved across policies and when selecting among proposed chunks improves closed-loop return. Across 65 locomotion, navigation, and manipulation tasks, ABI's chunk critic guides weak imitation policies to match or surpass zero-shot RL baselines with high sample efficiency, outperforms existing zero-shot critics on identical proposals, and improves externally trained RL actors without retraining. From raw pixels, ABI delivers substantial guidance gains and surpasses prior zero-shot RL baselines on visual manipulation, highlighting its potential for visuomotor control.

SWEEP-Bench: Do Embodied Policies Act on the Speed They See?
Hiroaki Honda, Koya Sakamoto, Shu Morikuni, Yusuke Iwasawa, Taiki Miyanishi
cs.RO · cs.CV · cs.LG
Abstract
Robot policies must adapt to the speed of moving objects, yet existing benchmarks rarely measure this ability across diverse tasks and speeds. We introduce SWEEP-Bench, a simulation benchmark with 80 conveyor-belt manipulation tasks spanning 16 skill categories, each evaluated at 13 belt speeds (0.10-0.40 m/s). Objects are transported through physical contact with a visibly moving belt. Each task has a static counterpart, and each evaluation episode uses the same randomized scene at all 13 speeds. We fine-tune eight vision-language-action and world-action models on demonstrations spanning the full speed range, comparing observations from the current frame alone with those including two past frames. For six models, the success rate peaks at intermediate speeds, and their failures indicate that they tend to produce actions suited to the average demonstration speed rather than to the actual one. Past frames raise the success rate by 10-40 percentage points for three models, and linear probes show that the belt speed is also most linearly decodable from these three. Adding ground-truth speed input to four of the models improves all of them, and a speed estimated from the images keeps most of this gain. These results show that SWEEP-Bench exposes speed-dependent failures and suggest that past frames help only policies from which the speed is most decodable, such as those pretrained on multiple frames. Project page: https://damin3927.github.io/SWEEP-Bench

cs.LG / 107 / 2611.30907
DexLatentWorld: 3D Cross-Embodiment Latent Action World Models for Zero-Shot Robotic Manipulation
Vinay Udit Mohan, Xuchuan Huang, Rolandos Alexandros Potamias
cs.RO · cs.CV · cs.LG
Abstract
World models facilitate planning and control in robotic manipulation by enabling agents to anticipate the consequences of their actions. However, they typically rely on action-labelled interaction data that is costly to acquire and difficult to scale. These models are also often tied to the specific embodiment they were trained on, limiting transferability to previously unseen robot morphologies. We introduce a 3D latent-action world model that learns continuous action representations directly from point-cloud observations of retargeted human manipulation demonstrations. A contrastive objective is used to encourage consistent representations of motion across embodiments. The resulting unified latent action space serves directly as the search space for model-predictive control, where sampled latent actions condition particle-based future predictions. Executable robot commands are then recovered from the predicted geometric motion without requiring an embodiment-specific action decoder. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate that the learned latent actions exhibit controllable and compositional motion, transfer to unseen robot embodiments, and support zero-shot manipulation with unseen gripper geometries. Following task-agnostic adaptation, our model achieves 90%, 92%, and 60% success on reaching, grasping, and placing, respectively, compared with DexWM's reported 72%, 58%, and 28%. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot real-world manipulation with an unseen dexterous hand, achieving an 86% success rate across 50 trials on five diverse tasks involving pushing, grasping, and lifting everyday objects. These results highlight the potential of geometry-grounded latent actions as a unified, transferable interface for world-model-based robotic manipulation. Project materials, including demonstration videos and source code, are available at https://vinaymohan0409.github.io/DexLatentWorld/.

cs.LG / 108 / 2611.31099
NoveltyGate: Novelty, Not Error, Decides Which VLA Prefix Tokens to Compute Exactly
Lemeng Qi
cs.RO · cs.LG
Abstract
Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $π_{0.5}$ re-encode the camera images and the instruction with a 2B-parameter backbone at every control step, and the feed-forward layers of this prefix account for most of its compute. A natural way to save this compute is to send most tokens through a low-rank MLP and compute exactly only the tokens whose approximation error is large. We find that this intuition is wrong. Even a verifier that knows every token's exact error picks the wrong tokens, producing 1.3--1.7$\times$ larger action deviation than a simple test of whether a token's input is novel, that is, whether it falls outside the subspace seen during calibration. Large errors concentrate in tokens the policy relies on little, such as the third-person camera, while the novelty test favors the wrist camera, a view the action depends on heavily. We call this the error--reliance gap. Building on it, we propose NoveltyGate, a training-free method that routes each prefix token, once per layer and before any multiplication, to either a low-rank or the original MLP. Deciding once per layer instead of once per matrix product avoids moving wide intermediate tensors and keeps every shape static, so the whole prefix runs as a single CUDA graph. On LIBERO, NoveltyGate accelerates the $π_{0.5}$ prefix by up to 1.61$\times$, stays 2.7--2.9$\times$ closer to the original policy than channel pruning and low-rank compression at equal compute, and preserves closed-loop task success.

cs.LG / 109 / 2611.30886
Vitrify Exact Learning: exact differential equations, changes of variable and closed forms from numerical data
Benedict Irwin, Alexander Mathiasen, Tom Etminan
cs.SC · cs.LG
Abstract
Symbolic regression searches a space of expression trees for a formula that fits data. Many functions of the sciences have no finite expression over the usual operations and still satisfy a linear differential equation with polynomial coefficients. Vitrify Exact Learning takes nu- merical values of a function and proceeds in three steps. It assumes that the function, in its own variable or after a change of variable or a pushforward of a density, is annihilated by an operator with polynomial coefficients. It finds that operator as the null vector of a matrix of weak-form measurements, in which the data are integrated against test functions and never differentiated, makes the coefficients exact, and tests the exact operator on data that the fit did not read against a noise level propagated from the data. It then solves the exact operator symbolically and keeps the closed form that matches the data. Each step has precedent; the combination takes values on an interval, from a quadrature, a float64 table or a sample, to an exact equation and a closed form. On noise-free benchmarks it recovers 45 of 53 classic targets, 108 of the 120 AI Feynman equations and 74.1% of the Feynman problems of SR- Bench, against 33, 69 and 55.8% for the best other programs, and 50 of 132 special-function targets generated after its code was frozen, against 23. From 40-digit values it returns Meijer G densities, hypergeometric forms for the deflection of light by a black hole, and Appell and Lauricella functions of two variables. With noise in several variables, with sparse data and for equations above fourth order it mostly returns no model.

cs.LG / 110 / 2611.30584
Do Candlestick Charts Suffice? The Incremental Economic Value of Technical Indicators in Stock Return Prediction
Peng Liu, Yanyan Zheng
econ.GN · cs.CE · cs.LG · q-fin.PM · q-fin.TR
Abstract
Although technical analysis remains widely used in practice, the need for manually constructed indicators is increasingly questioned as deep learning models can extract features directly from OHLC price data. This paper examines the standalone economic value of trading volume and manually constructed technical-indicator groups and whether adding these groups to OHLC candlestick charts provides incremental economic value. Using daily data for 1,707 Chinese A-share stocks from 2013 to 2025, we construct approximately 3.36 million stock-window samples and encode them as multi-channel images containing candlestick charts, trading volume, and seven widely used manually constructed technical indicators. The primary analysis uses a 2D CNN on these images; complementary tests apply a logistic regression, a 1D CNN, and an LSTM to numerical representations of the same samples. Out-of-sample performance from 2021 to 2025 is evaluated using decile portfolios, Sharpe ratios, Fama--French alphas, and formal pairwise tests. Our empirical results yield two central findings. First, specifications based separately on OHLC, trading volume, and each technical-indicator group produce significantly positive high-minus-low returns and factor-adjusted alphas, together with economically meaningful Sharpe ratios; the OHLC-only specifications generally perform best under the nonlinear models. Second, adding these technical-indicator groups to OHLC does not systematically improve any of these performance measures in our setting. Together, these results provide the first large-scale evidence from the Chinese A-share market on the standalone and incremental economic value of these technical-indicator groups across multiple representations and model architectures.

cs.LG / 111 / 2611.30198
Geospatial foundation models and deep learning for climate resilience: a review of transfer, uncertainty and decision readiness
Parastoo Farajpoor, Mohammadreza Narimani
eess.IV · cs.LG · physics.ao-ph · physics.geo-ph · stat.AP
Abstract
Geospatial foundation models can reuse information learned from large Earth-observation archives, but their value for climate resilience depends on whether that information transfers to unfamiliar events, regions and observing conditions. This review connects advances in deep learning with the evidence needed for hazard monitoring and early warning. A descriptive audit of 137 full-text hazard-application studies is interpreted alongside a separate corpus of 37 model and benchmark records. Ninety-eight application studies reported an out-of-distribution experiment, whereas headline evaluations included held-out events in 31 studies, regions in 25 and sensors in only two. None of the ten studies coded for geospatial foundation-model fine-tuning used sensor holdout as a headline test. Uncertainty-related methods were recorded in 16 studies, including two with explicitly calibrated probabilistic output. These overlapping counts describe evaluation practice within the coded corpus, not a ranking of model families. We distinguish Earth-observation representation learning from atmospheric forecasting and examine how labels, observability, forecast lead time and decision requirements constrain their contribution across flood, wildfire, drought, heat, cryosphere and cascading-hazard applications. We then develop a decision-backward evaluation framework: define the action and information available when it must be taken, reproduce the relevant shift, retain a matched task-specific baseline, and report misses, false alarms, reliability and end-to-end latency. The framework turns transferability from a broad model claim into a testable requirement for climate adaptation and risk management.

Demographic Encoding is Not Exposure: Fairness and Privacy in Chest X-ray Foundation Models
Sahar Askari, Amin Golnari
eess.IV · cs.CV · cs.LG
Abstract
Medical foundation models encode patient demographics and can reveal whether a patient was in the training set, and these properties are often treated as one problem. We tested whether they are aligned by measuring demographic encoding, diagnostic fairness gaps and membership-inference vulnerability on the same models. We trained 200 linear or multilayer-perceptron (MLP) heads on frozen BiomedCLIP, DINOv2 and RAD-DINO embeddings, with three seeds, and audited them on CheXpert and NIH ChestX-ray14. Demographic encoding explained almost no variance in patient vulnerability, and all 72 CheXpert associations were statistically equivalent to zero. Erasing linearly decodable demographics left leakage unchanged but reduced age-related underdiagnosis gaps. Leakage depended instead on head capacity and training length. On RAD-DINO, a linear head reached a membership-inference area under the curve (AUC) of 0.694, compared with 0.907 for a 30-epoch MLP, at similar test performance. Fairness and privacy should therefore be audited separately, and linear heads or shorter training reduce leakage with little or no loss of utility. The code is available on GitHub for public use.

cs.LG / 113 / 2611.31127
Data-Driven Identification of Uncertainty Sets with Conformance Guarantees
Laura Lützow, Mykel J. Kochenderfer, Matthias Althoff
eess.SY · cs.LG
Abstract
Formal verification and controller synthesis require accurate models. Conformance relations specify the required accuracy of a model such that properties established for the model carry over to the target system. Existing methods for establishing them from measured data are typically restricted to a single relation, a specific model class, or a downstream verification algorithm. We present ConfID, a unified framework that establishes reachset, trace, and simulation conformance with respect to measured traces by identifying uncertainty sets for a given, possibly nonlinear nominal model. Unmodeled effects are thus captured by nondeterminism rather than by refining the nominal dynamics. For all three conformance relations, the identification is a linear program that minimizes the size of the reachable sets; only its constraints depend on the relation. We further derive distribution-free bounds on the probability that the identified models are conformant for unseen behaviors. Experiments on simulated and real-world data evaluate the models identified for the three relations, confirm the guarantees, and show that these models cover unseen behaviors more reliably than baselines, with comparable or smaller sets.

Lorentz symmetry in self-supervised representation learning
Andreas Hermansen, Tobias Golling, Slava Voloshynovskiy
hep-ph · cs.LG
Abstract
Self-supervised learning (SSL) and explicit physical inductive biases have driven major advances in jet tagging, yet they are typically pursued along separate tracks. In this work, we unify both paradigms by integrating the Lorentz-equivariant Geometric Algebra Transformer slim (L-GATr-slim) architecture with the LeJEPA framework for representation learning. Pre-training on 100 million jets from the JetClass dataset, we optimize towards a latent space, which is invariant across physics-motivated jet augmentations. We demonstrate that enforcing Lorentz symmetry in the latent space is critical for representation quality and that this can be achieved either architecturally or learned via kinematic augmentations. With a standard non-invariant Transformer backbone, LeJEPA outperforms established autoregressive, masked particle modelling, and self-distillation baselines in linear- and MLP-probe accuracy, with L-GATr-slim providing further complementary gains. Across downstream benchmarks, our pre-trained models consistently outperform baselines trained from scratch or through different pre-training objectives.

cs.LG / 115 / 2611.29725
Continuous-Time LQR from a Single Discrete-Time Off-Policy Batch
Chaorui Yao, Yuhua Zhu
math.OC · cs.LG
Abstract
We study discounted continuous-time linear--quadratic regulation (LQR) with unknown drift parameters and additive noise, using a single batch of discrete-time off-policy transitions. Discrete-time methods target a policy tied to the training interval, while shortening this interval can make learning from finite data more sensitive to noise. Learning an accurate continuous-time controller therefore requires balancing discretization and finite-sample errors while preserving stability throughout policy improvement. We develop a drift-only policy iteration algorithm, termed PhiBE-PI, using one quadratic state--action critic for policy evaluation and explicit greedy improvement. Reusing the batch makes later policies depend on the data. Exploiting the quadratic structure of LQR, we show that the data enter every policy evaluation only through one policy-independent empirical matrix, so a single high-probability bound controls all iterates. For sufficiently large discount~$β$, small observation intervals, and a sufficiently large batch, we prove that all iterates are stabilizing for the discounted problem and converge quadratically to a data-dependent fixed point. The gain bound separates iteration, finite-sample, and discretization errors. In this regime, the finite-sample and discretization terms scale as $1/(β\sqrt{nΔt})$ and $Δt/β$, respectively. The bounds thus reveal a tradeoff: at a fixed batch size, finer observations reduce discretization error but increase finite-sample error. Because PhiBE-PI approximates the continuous-time optimal gain rather than a discrete-time one, its policy can remain near-optimal when deployed at faster control rates. Experiments confirm this advantage over discrete-time Bellman-equation baselines when the observation interval is small relative to the system's time scale.

cs.LG / 116 / 2611.29841
Sharp Asymptotic Theory of Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Gaussian Processes with a Matern Kernel
Ameer Qaqish, Sudipto Banerjee, Didong Li
math.ST · cs.LG · math.PR · stat.ML
Abstract
Gaussian processes (GPs) provide a flexible framework for modeling complex dependence structures through a covariance function, or kernel, whose parameters determine the variability, correlation, and smoothness of the underlying process. The Matérn kernel is among the most popular choices due to its flexibility in modeling different degrees of smoothness. Although the identifiability of Matérn kernel parameters under fixed-domain asymptotics is completely understood, identifiability alone does not establish the consistency or asymptotic behavior of the maximum likelihood estimators (MLEs) routinely used in practice. In this paper, we address this gap by developing a sharp asymptotic theory for the joint MLE of Matérn kernel parameters. Since parameter identifiability depends critically on the dimension of the observation domain, we characterize the estimable parameters and establish their convergence rates across different dimensions. We establish joint asymptotic normality and minimax optimality of the convergence rates. In addition, we establish asymptotically valid confidence regions for the estimable parameters. Our results accommodate irregular sampling designs and extend to sub-Gaussian measurement errors. Extensive simulation studies illustrate the theoretical results.

Topological analysis of permeability tensor in anisotropic porous media
Rafał Topolnicki, Paweł Dłotko, Maciej Matyka
physics.comp-ph · cs.LG · physics.flu-dyn
Abstract
The permeability of an anisotropic porous medium is a tensor whose off-diagonal components, which describe the deflection of the macroscopic flux away from the driving force, are small and change sign under reflections. We ask whether direction-aware topological data analysis can predict the full permeability tensor of three-dimensional porous media directly from their geometry. We introduce two direction-aware topological descriptors for flow problems: a cone-based filtration, adapted from our earlier work on the elastic stiffness tensor, and a throat-scale filtration built on the distance transform of the pore space. Using permeability tensors computed with the lattice Boltzmann method, we compare them with a comprehensive set of non-topological baselines, comprising statistical microstructure descriptors and physics-based permeability estimators. The topological descriptors are most informative for the off-diagonal components, which the baselines capture least well. There the throat-scale filtration alone outperforms every non-topological descriptor set, including the union of all statistical descriptors and physics-based estimators, and adding it to the baselines consistently improves the prediction. We also confirm the approach on real rock data.

cs.LG / 118 / 2611.30955
LeCellModel: Interpretable Density Estimation over the Gene Expression Manifold
Gil Karin, Artemii Bakulin, Nir Yosef
q-bio.GN · cs.LG
Abstract
Representation learning for single-cell RNA-seq has been evaluated by the identities representations capture -- cell types, lineages, perturbations -- rather than how faithfully they model the distribution of cell states on the gene expression manifold. As a result, density estimation, rare-state detection, perturbation scoring, and gene-level attribution are bolted onto frozen embeddings as separate models, disconnected from the geometry of the data. We argue that modeling the distribution of cell states should be the primary objective, and that representation quality follows from it. Building on LeJEPA, whose SIGReg objective enforces a provably optimal isotropic Gaussian latent, we introduce LeCellModel, which reads the encoder's Jacobian log-volume (JEPA-SCORE) under this Gaussian latent as a relative typicality score. Across several datasets, LeCellModel outperforms established methods on the scIB benchmark for representation quality. Furthermore, we show that LeCellModel enables detection of rare expression states using JEPA-SCORE as a typicality measure, applying it to a controlled cytokine panel, where it identifies stimulated cells across minority fractions and tracks pathway-response magnitude. We introduce gene-level interpretability of the typicality score -- to our knowledge, the first method for analyzing JEPA-SCORE in feature space. Leveraging this framework, LeCellModel recapitulates the known association of a profibrotic macrophage program with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, and discovers a CD177+ activated regulatory T cell subpopulation previously described only in tumor contexts. Both findings emerge directly from the geometry of the learned embedding, without relying on supervised annotations.

cs.LG / 119 / 2611.30789
Quantum resources constrain function approximation
Oxana Shaya, Lirandë Pira
quant-ph · cs.LG
Abstract
Universal function approximation is central to machine learning. Quantum learning models are universal as well, but this does not specify the resources needed to approximate a given function. We study how coherence, imaginarity, entanglement and magic constrain function approximation for a fixed encoding and readout, using the cumulative resource power of the trainable gates. In a one-qubit model with phase encoding, coherence bounds the oscillation of the model function, while imaginarity bounds its odd part. In a two-qubit model, entanglement bounds the distance from product functions. These bounds hold at any encoding depth. For magic, the phase encoding itself supplies non-Clifford operations. On domains bounded away from zero, Clifford trainable gates suffice for uniform approximation. Replacing unrestricted trainable gates by Clifford gates increases the encoding depth at most polynomially in the original depth, the inverse error and the inverse distance of the domain from zero. Magic in the trainable gates can nevertheless improve accuracy at fixed depth. These results show how the resources of a quantum model must match the structure of the target function.

cs.LG / 120 / 2611.30635
Robust Mixture Regressions and EM Algorithms via the Log-Truncated Likelihood
Huiming Zhang, Longkun Hao
stat.ME · cs.LG · math.ST
Abstract
Finite mixture regression is sensitive to gross residual outliers when component errors are modeled by Gaussian likelihoods. We propose a log-truncated likelihood for mixture regression. The likelihood is obtained by integrating a logarithmically growing Catoni-type score and exponentiating the negative integrated score, producing a proper location-scale density with a reusable normalizing constant and EM-compatible responsibilities. Although the induced density itself is lighter than exponential and has all moments, its likelihood score grows only logarithmically; this distinction yields a smooth residual-robust estimator that can be stably fitted when the data are generated from Laplace, Pareto, or even infinite-variance heavy-tailed error mechanisms. We derive deterministic tail envelopes, the location-scale decomposition of the normalizing constant, a rejection sampler, a lower-bounded mixing-weight update, a unique componentwise scale update, and a constrained generalized EM algorithm. The theory gives monotonicity of the observed likelihood and a local population-to-sample perturbation guarantee under standard compactness, contraction, and numerical-accuracy conditions. Simulations and applications to insurance claim severity and crypto return innovations show that the method is a competitive smooth likelihood-based alternative to Gaussian and pseudo-robust EM procedures, especially in residual-outlier regimes, while also clarifying its limitations under high leverage and extremely adversarial contamination.

cs.LG / 121 / 2611.30706
Bayesian sequential decision-making for adaptive early warning of bridge failure risk
Teng Li, James L. Beck, Yong Huang, Hui Li, Hongju Han
stat.ME · cs.LG
Abstract
As a critical functionality of structural health monitoring (SHM) systems, early warning of increased bridge failure risk is essential for structural safety. However, traditional methods treat early warning merely as passive detection against a fixed safety limit and neglect evolving uncertainties and the economic consequences of decisions, leading to delayed alarms that increase the failure risk and hinder reliable and rational decision-making. This study formulates the early warning of increased structural failure risk as a sequential decision-making problem and develops a Bayesian framework for its solution. The presented framework unifies a probabilistic state transition model, an observation prediction model, cost models for early warning decisions, and a threshold-based decision strategy into a closed loop encompassing update, prediction, optimization, and decision execution. The structural state is updated iteratively via Bayes' theorem upon the arrival of new monitoring data, ensuring each decision is conditioned on the latest information. Through pre-posterior analysis over predicted future observations, the warning threshold is optimized by minimizing the expected total cost, which explicitly balances structural failure risks against warning response costs. In this way, the warning paradigm is shifted from passive detection to proactive decision-making, with the warning threshold adaptively updated as uncertainties and costs evolve. The framework was verified via two bridge case studies covering typical scenarios that lead to increased structural failure risk, including steel truss member fracture and stay cable rupture. Results demonstrate that warning decisions can be triggered in a timely and effective manner before severe consequences occur.

Tabular Foundation Models for Weighted Regression and Classification
Junwen Xia, Yan He, Dehan Kong, Zhenhua Lin
stat.ML · cs.LG
Abstract
Weighted regression and classification have applications ranging from missing-data analysis and causal inference to insurance pricing and particle physics. Existing weighted methods must be fitted and tuned on each dataset, which is costly for flexible nonlinear learners. Tabular foundation models avoid this cost. A Transformer is pretrained once on many simulated datasets and then predicts on a new dataset by in-context learning, using its observations as context without further fitting. Recent models such as TabPFN-3.5 surpass tuned conventional methods, but they cannot use sample weights. We develop a general pipeline that adapts such models to weighted prediction through weighted attention, a normalized weighted loss, and pretraining on synthetic weighted prediction tasks from missing-data problems. Applied to TabPFN-3.5, it yields WeightedPFN, which performs strongly on real datasets, both in missing-data problems and in out-of-distribution causal tasks, while running about as fast as linear baselines. We also establish a statistical theory showing that a suitably pretrained weighted Transformer attains the nonparametric minimax rate for weighted regression on new datasets without further fitting.

Hoang-Son Tran, Pranav Gupta, Subhroshekhar Ghosh
stat.ML · cs.LG · math.PR
Abstract
We construct wavelet-based determinantal samplers on manifolds and geometric graphs whose approximation rates adapt to the regularity of the observable. On a Riemannian manifold of dimension $m$, our wavelet DPPs satisfy variance reduction of order $n^{1-2s/m}$ for linear statistics of both $s$-Hölder and $H^s$ observables, where $0<s\le1$. Using these samplers, we further construct unbiased quadrature rules with root mean square error $O(n^{-1/2-s/m})$ using at most $3n/2$ function evaluations, matching the classical optimal randomized integration exponent. For point clouds sampled from an $m$-dimensional manifold, we develop corresponding determinantal samplers on two standard classes of geometric random graphs: $\varepsilon$-graphs and symmetric $k$-nearest-neighbour graphs. These samplers satisfy the same variance reduction for linear statistics of $s$-Hölder observables and yield conditionally unbiased estimators of empirical averages with root mean square error $O(n^{-1/2-s/m})$, using at most $2n$ function evaluations. In both settings, the rates are governed by the intrinsic dimension $m$ and the regularity $s$ of the observable.

Statistically Optimal and Near Linear Time Hypothesis Selection
Satyen Kale, Amirreza Shaeiri, Kunal Talwar
stat.ML · cs.LG · math.ST
Abstract
In hypothesis selection we are given $n$ distributions $q_1,\dots,q_n$ on a countable domain $\mathcal{X}$ and samples from an unknown distribution $p$. The goal is a distribution $q$ with $\mathrm{TV}(p,q)\leα\min_i\mathrm{TV}(p,q_i)+ε$. The factor $α=2$ is optimal for algorithms using a number of samples from $p$ that is independent of $|\mathcal{X}|$, and in general only improper learners achieve it. We give a learner that achieves $α=2$ with $O(\log(n/δ)/ε^2)$ samples of $p$, with probability at least $1-δ$. This matches the sample complexity of Yatracos's factor-$3$ estimator, and it removes the logarithmic factors in the factor-$2$ bound of Bousquet et al. (FOCS 2021). The learner accesses the $q_i$ only through sampling and pointwise comparisons. We measure its running time by its oracle complexity, the number of oracle calls. In expectation it makes $O((nε^{-2}+ε^{-4}\log(1/ε))\log(n/δ))$ oracle calls, independent of $\mathcal{X}$. It runs multiplicative weights over the constraints $\mathrm{TV}(q,q_i)\le\mathrm{TV}(p,q_i)$ and uses at most one sample of $p$ per round.

cs.LG / 125 / 2611.30006
Sequential Selection against an Adaptive Opponent
Zhongyuan Lyu, Xiaocong Xu
stat.ML · cs.LG · math.ST · stat.ME
Abstract
Selecting a strategy by testing it against an opponent is common in game-playing AI, red-teaming of language models, and safety evaluations of AI agents. In many of these settings, the opponent adapts to what it observes, so a strategy that keeps winning in practice may already have stopped working by the time it is used. Motivated by these settings, we study a player who tries strategies in practice games against an adaptive opponent, decides when to stop, and then either selects one strategy for the next game or abstains. The goal is to select a strategy that meets a target win probability while rarely selecting one that has already fallen below it. For a single strategy, we propose the Sequential Private Accumulated-excess Rule (SPAR), which accumulates evidence through a capped likelihood ratio and selects the strategy once this evidence reaches a privately drawn uniform threshold. We show that the stopping time must involve such private randomness. The number of games SPAR needs is inversely proportional to the error tolerance, and this rate is optimal even when the opponent happens not to adapt. To select among multiple strategies, we introduce Screen-then-SPAR, which screens candidates in stages before applying SPAR. The procedure adapts to the best strategy's unknown initial margin above the target and achieves the minimax rate up to logarithmic factors. The performance of Screen-then-SPAR is demonstrated through simulations and two real-data studies, one using recorded coding-agent attacks from MonitoringBench and the other using rock-paper-scissors matches between human players and an adaptive bot.

cs.LG / 126 / 2611.30044
The response field approach to path integral control
George Stamatescu
stat.ML · cond-mat.stat-mech · cs.LG · math.OC
Abstract
This paper investigates non-linear path integral control problems within the response field formalism of nonequilibrium field theory. The aim of this work is exploratory, based on the identification of correspondences between backward adjoint processes and the response field of non-equilibrium statistical physics, whose properties have not been set out in an optimal control setting. The response field is found to play an analogous role to the backward adjoint process under the stochastic maximum principle. In particular, the gradient of the optimal cost-to-go at the initial time, which is proportional to the optimal control, is given by the average of the response field at the initial time. In contrast to the case of non-equilibrium dynamics, the response function is found to be acausal in the control setting. The linear-quadratic case of path integral control is studied, confirming it as the free theory, meaning that solving the control problem is equivalent to completing the square and determining the propagator for a two point boundary value problem. The developments presented here are a necessary prelude to applications based on field theoretic approximation, for both path integral control and their dual inference problems.

Seokhun Park, Kunwoong Kim, Yongdai Kim
stat.ML · cs.LG
Abstract
Functional ANOVA models express a prediction as a sum of main effects and interactions, but existing neural functional ANOVA models require the interactions to be specified in advance, which forces a trade-off between missing higher-order structure and the cost of enumerating many interactions. We propose SCAN (Scalable Component Additive Networks), which learns which features each basis function combines, so that components of different orders are selected and estimated jointly without enumerating candidates. The learned component index sets form a small candidate collection on which post-hoc identification is carried out efficiently. A global component-selection parameter shares information across basis functions, and truncating negligible component-selection weights gives a sparse model that is identified after training. We establish universal approximation, a minimax optimal rate up to a logarithmic factor, and component selection consistency, which together imply that the discovered components contain all identified true components with probability tending to one. In synthetic experiments, SCAN learns components whose maximum order is close to the true one, and recovers higher-order components more accurately than the baseline models, with post-hoc identification taking a few seconds for 100 inputs. SCAN also outperforms most neural functional ANOVA models in prediction on the benchmark datasets and trains at a much lower cost than exhaustive second-order models. We also apply SCAN to predict treatment response in breast cancer from 12,502 gene-expression variables.

Precise Asymptotics of Non-Convex M-Estimators
Shirley Xiaoqi Liu, Tirthankar Adhikari, Parthe Pandit
stat.ML · cs.IT · cs.LG
Abstract
Precise asymptotic theory for M-estimators in high-dimensional settings is largely limited to convex or mildly non-convex formulations, yet non-convex loss functions as well as regularizers are widely used in practice. We study M-estimation in generalized linear models (GLMs) where the loss function or the regularizer can be non-convex. Under rotationally invariant design matrices in the proportional asymptotic regime, we analyze the problem through Vector Approximate Message Passing (VAMP), whose iterates are described by a low-dimensional deterministic recursion called State Evolution (SE). Existing proofs of SE require the proximal operators of the loss function and the regularizer to be Lipschitz, but a non-convex loss or regularizer can have a discontinuous proximal operator, and the usual Onsager terms in VAMP then miss the contribution of the discontinuities. Assuming that the proximal operators are special functions of locally bounded variation, we derive a correction to the Onsager terms using a distributional Stein's lemma. We prove that SE holds for the corrected VAMP. We apply the theory to analyze group sparse regression with an $\ell_0$-type penalty and to robust regression with the Cauchy loss.

Fast and Consistent Structure Learning in Graphical Models via Approximate Cross-Validation
Zhao Lyu, Mladen Kolar, Bryon Aragam
stat.ML · cs.LG · stat.CO · stat.ME
Abstract
Structure learning for sparse graphical models in high dimensions requires both computational scalability and selection consistency. Classical criteria such as (Extended) Bayesian Information Criterion can provide consistency, but rely on model-specific likelihoods and complexity calibration. In comparison, cross-validation avoids such analytic calibration and is therefore attractive for graph learning. However, cross-validation is computationally infeasible and theoretically inconsistent in structure learning. This creates a tension between consistency and flexibility in modeling. In this work, we resolve the tension by developing a scalable graph-recovery procedure built on approximate cross-validation. We demonstrate its effectiveness in learning large graphical models both theoretically and empirically, and establish selection consistency under mild signal strength assumptions.

cs.LG / 130 / 2611.30937
A theory of inductive node-level generalization from a single large graph
Nicolas Keriven, Yann Viegas
stat.ML · cs.LG
Abstract
In Graph Machine Learning (GML), the notion of generalization fundamentally varies depending on the task level and the properties of the dataset. For instance, graph-level tasks fit into the traditional ML framework of i.i.d. samples, with relatively small graphs. On the contrary, node-level tasks involve dependent nodes, often in a few large graphs. Existing studies often consider the transductive settings, where training and test data co-exist in the same graph, or, for inductive learning, try to recover some kind of probabilistic ``independence'', e.g. by still assuming a large number of independent graphs or subgraphs. In this work, we develop a novel framework to express the generalization capabilities of Graph ML algorithms for inductive node-level tasks when learning from a single large graph, taking inspiration from the literature on GNN transferability. In particular, we emphasize the similarities with classical ML by revisiting the excess risk decomposition with a new notion of ``transferable'' risk on large graphs. We apply this framework to Latent Position random graphs: we uncover new insights on the hardness of GML compared to traditional ML, and derive novel notions of concentration. Finally, we apply this framework to several models of GNNs, unifying several existing results on GNNs transferability and universality.

Prediction-Powered Regression via Calibration: Beyond the Supervised Minimax Benchmark
Jin Su, Yong Zhou, Jian Huang
stat.ML · cs.LG
Abstract
We study nonparametric regression with limited labeled data and abundant observations carrying potentially inaccurate pseudo-labels. Our proposed method, weighted prediction-powered regression via calibration (wPPRC), first calibrates pseudo-labels using labeled data, then fits a predictor by weighted regression using observed and calibrated responses. Over Hölder classes, we derive nonasymptotic excess-risk bounds for clipped ReLU estimators and establish a minimax lower bound for the corresponding regression problem. Under suitable conditions, the upper and lower bounds match up to logarithmic factors. Moreover, wPPRC can achieve a worst-case risk of smaller order than the minimax risks under four baseline observation structures on the same joint distribution class, demonstrating the value of additional pseudo-labels. We also construct a validation-selected (VS) estimator using an independent labeled validation sample to choose the weight. The VS estimator satisfies an expected-risk oracle inequality and preserves the improvement over the baseline minimax risks with the same total labeled-data budget. Simulations and an application to predicting homeless counts illustrate the gains of the proposed estimators.

cs.NE / 1 / 2611.30277
A New Perspective on ANN-to-SNN Conversion: Hardware-Aligned Multi-Threshold Neuron Dynamics for Neuromorphic Inference
Shaohong Gu, Jiyuan Zhang, Yimeng Shan, Chenxiao Dou, Wei Hua, Malu Zhang, Honglin Cao, Choonghyun Lee, Jingwei Chen
cs.NE · cs.AI
Abstract
By accumulating spikes over multiple timesteps, rate coding approximates the real-valued activations of an ANN, a principle that underpins numerous ANN-to-SNN conversion methods. However, the converted SNNs typically incur loss in accuracy compared to the original ANN. Existing methods either increase a number of timesteps or introduce more complex neuronal dynamics to reduce this accuracy gap. Yet, both approaches ultimately lead to the same outcome: redundancy either in information or in computation, thereby suffering from efficiency degradation. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{PRIME} (\underline{P}otential-\underline{R}esidual \underline{I}ntegration for \underline{M}ulti-threshold \underline{E}ncoding), a multi-threshold concurrent spiking neuron framework redesigned from a hardware data representation perspective:a) We introduce the Residual Membrane Potential Amplification (RMPA) mechanism, which replaces rate coding with Integration Coding by actively amplifying the residual membrane potential. RMPA enables the binary representation of spikes to carry substantially more information, achieving near-lossless conversion with as few as two timesteps.b) Complementarily, we implement concurrent spike firing in multi-threshold neurons, where spikes are decoded directly from the binary representation of floating-point data, eliminating membrane potential--threshold comparisons and replacing multiplications with lightweight bit-shift and accumulation operations that align with hardware computation primitives. At $T=2$ and $D=3$, we achieve competitive performance across both vision and language benchmarks with only 40.6\% of the FP32 bit-transmission cost and 13.4\% of the FP32 multiplication energy consumption. The PRIME framework establishes a new design principle for efficient ANN-to-SNN conversion, bridging the gap between algorithmic efficiency and hardware constraints.

The Stigmergic Index: A Biomimetic Edge Centrality for Spatial Network Analysis
Sofiane Madmar, Didier Josselin, Vincent Labatut, Muhammad Zaly Shah, Olivier Blight
cs.NE
Abstract
Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) is a family of metaheuristics inspired by the pheromone-based navigation of real ants, a decentralized mechanism often associated with shortest-path discovery. Over the past two decades, research has primarily focused on optimization tasks such as vehicle routing within a network. In this paper, we shift this perspective by using swarm intelligence to gather diagnostic information about the underlying network structure itself. Through decentralized exploration, we harness stigmergic dynamics to introduce a novel topological and behavioural metric: the Stigmergic Index. While sharing baseline structural properties with traditional betweenness centrality on simple grids, our index accounts for path polarization effects that can diverge from shortest-path-based assumptions.

MF-EDA: Joining Membership Functions to Adapt the Number of Distributions in Gaussian Estimation-of-Distribution Algorithms
Jun Zhang, Tong Qian, Hua Ding, Wei-Jie Yu, Xiao-Fang Liu, Jian-Yu Li
cs.NE · cs.AI
Abstract
An estimation-of-distribution algorithm (EDA) usually samples from one Gaussian, whose peak sits where most selected individuals are. On a landscape with two funnels that is not where the best solutions are: the wider funnel supplies most of the selected individuals, and the deeper funnel, which holds the global optimum, is lost early. This paper builds the search distribution as a neuro-fuzzy system builds a model: from Gaussian membership functions joined by membership degrees. In every generation the proposed MF-EDA searches the principal directions of the selected individuals for the direction along which they are bimodal, describes them on that direction by one or two membership functions according to the Bayesian information criterion and a separation test, joins each membership function to a local Gaussian in the other directions, and samples from the normalised union. A membership function has height one whatever the number of individuals under it, so a detected funnel receives samples according to its width. A two-region selection model shows that sampling shares proportional to the head count, as in a Gaussian mixture, compound the early disadvantage of the deeper funnel, and that the union does not. With one membership function the algorithm is its single-Gaussian baseline; the steps cost no fitness evaluations but make a generation 8 to 17 times slower to compute. On 36 double-funnel settings the component raises the successful runs of a rank-weighted Gaussian EDA from 805 to 1712 of 1800. On the Lunacek double funnel in 30 dimensions it raises that EDA from 4 to 49 and AMaLGaM from 0 to 47 successes in 50 runs, while results on single-funnel functions and on ten multimodal BBOB functions do not change. Restarted CMA-ES remains cheaper in evaluations on the standard double funnel, and the component stops helping when the global funnel is much narrower than the other.

cs.NE / 4 / 2611.30079
Designing Incoherent Multispectral Diffractive Optical Networks for Satellite Image Classification
Xilin Yang, Md Sadman Sakib Rahman, Ryan Lee, Aydogan Ozcan
physics.optics · cs.NE · physics.app-ph
Abstract
Optical neural networks and diffractive optical computing provide a promising route for performing task-specific inference with high parallelism and lightweight electronic post-processing. These advantages are especially attractive for multispectral satellite imaging, where conventional workflows rely on transmitting high-dimensional image cubes to the ground for downstream electronic analysis. Here, we introduce a computationally efficient surrogate model-guided framework for designing incoherent multispectral diffractive optical networks that directly output class probabilities onboard, eliminating the need to capture and transfer the full multispectral data cube for ground-side inference. We first train a physically compatible surrogate model, represented by a non-negative fully connected model that accommodates a generalized detector readout, yielding a task-specific non-negative multispectral intensity transformation that can be transferred to an optical processor. We then synthesize its diffractive counterpart through data-free point-spread-function-based optimization under spatially incoherent illumination. Using this approach, we numerically demonstrate a six-spectral-channel diffractive classifier for tri-class satellite-scene recognition, achieving a blind-testing accuracy of 79.8% for artificial surface, water body, and vegetated land images, closely approaching the 81.8% accuracy of its surrogate. We further demonstrate a more compact three-spectral-channel design that numerically achieves 72.7% blind-testing accuracy, compared with 75.1% for its corresponding surrogate model. This surrogate model-guided strategy provides a practical pathway for designing compact, task-specific incoherent multispectral optical processors for resource-constrained remote-sensing inference.

cs.CL / 1 / 2611.29750
Refine, Don't Reinvent: RASA-Bench for Source-Grounded Hindi Prose Refinement
Abdur Rahman, Pratham Singla, Mohammad Saifullah, Vasu Sharma
cs.CL · cs.AI
Abstract
For a producer of Hindi creative prose, drafting is cheap and editing is not: a machine-written episode, story, or essay reads as under-written and flat, laced with translationese, and it sometimes quietly alters what the source says. RASA-Bench targets that editing task across three Hindi prose forms, measuring how well a model refines an under-written AI draft, a task distinct from writing from scratch. Across 2,050 drafts and eight refiners (16,400 rewrites), a four-layer protocol credits a rewrite only after it passes a faithfulness check against its own source, then ranks the survivors by holistic editorial preference through per-form Bradley-Terry fits whose centered coefficients are standardized before equal-weight averaging. Staying faithful proves to be a decisive test that behaves differently by form: gate-failure rates range from 9.1% on short stories to 29.5% on audio fiction, and the drift that disqualifies a rewrite shifts from events and identity in narrative to claims and evidence in essays. A 600-case human audit puts gate agreement at 0.925 (0.91 to 0.94 across forms), whereas subjective preference is form-sensitive and least settled for essays, among human readers no less than the model judge. The benchmark, evaluation protocol, and Hindi prose diagnostics are available at https://abdur75648.github.io/rasa-bench.

ComplexIF: A Challenging Multi-Turn, Multi-Constraint Instruction-Following Benchmark
Zhichao Xu, Bingsen Chen, Yawei Wang, Tao Li, Haoyu Wang, Dan Roth, Vivek Srikumar
cs.CL
Abstract
As frontier LLMs saturate existing instruction-following benchmarks, measuring further progress requires harder tests that remain faithful to real use. In practice, users often combine several constraints, add them at different turns of a conversation, and expect all of them to hold in the assistant's response. We introduce ComplexIF, a challenging benchmark for this setting, together with the automatic pipeline that generates it. The pipeline expands seed requests into multi-turn conversations, weaves constraints into their turns, and keeps only tasks that a strong model can solve, so difficulty can be raised by adding constraints or turns while every task stays solvable. ComplexIF's two splits test complementary sides of instruction following: a verifiable split of format constraints, checked by programs, and a rubric split of semantic instructions, such as a tone or an audience, checked with an LLM judge. Across 14 proprietary and open-weight models, even the strongest satisfies every constraint on fewer than half of the verifiable tasks, and no model leads on both splits.
